idiom_name: capability interfaces with generic bounds, type tokens and pattern-matching switch
implementation_notes: Java has no type-level dispatch and erases generic type arguments, so a descriptor has to be hand-built from three pieces: a capability interface with a generic bound (<T extends Comparable<? super T>>, with Comparator<? super T> supplied from outside as the external description), a reifiable type token where the property is not expressible as an interface (Map<Class<?>, Handler>, Class.isAssignableFrom, or Gafter's anonymous subclass super type token - Guava's TypeToken - when the generic type itself matters), and, since Java 21, a switch over type patterns for a closed set of types (JEP 441). The classic descriptor therefore has no single Java counterpart: selection happens through nominal interfaces at compile time or through explicit tokens at runtime, and either way the mapping is written by hand and cannot be retrofitted onto a type that does not implement the interface.
pitfalls: Erasure: List<String>.class is not a type token at all and a Class<T> token carries only the raw type, so a Class-keyed table cannot tell List<String> from List<Integer>; the super type token (anonymous subclass plus getGenericSuperclass) is the workaround and it is reflective and fragile.

instanceof and pattern switches cannot test a type parameter (v instanceof T is a compile error) and v instanceof List accepts every element type, so the compiler emits unchecked warnings precisely where the trait stopped being statically checked.

A Class-keyed registry needs an explicit precedence rule (exact class, then nearest supertype) and a defined miss behaviour, because isAssignableFrom also returns true for interface implementations that were never described.
